Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
- Assessment summary:
  - Acute onset (3 days) watery progressing to very loose diarrhoea with frequent stools and profuse vomiting, subjective high fever, intermittent periumbilical crampy abdominal pain and urgency.
  - Household contact (brother) with similar symptoms and reported school outbreak — supports infectious etiology.
  - Unable to retain oral rehydration solution effectively; passed urine ~1 hour prior (subjective), suggesting not yet severely dehydrated but at risk.
  - No blood in stool reported. No prior GI disease.
- DDx-supported diagnostic reasoning (consistent with transcript):
  - Viral gastroenteritis (e.g., norovirus) — High likelihood: matches acute vomiting, watery diarrhoea, fever, household outbreak. (Supported by DDx.)
  - Bacterial gastroenteritis — Moderate likelihood: ongoing symptoms >48–72 hours and failure to improve with oral rehydration raise possibility; clinician recommended stool testing. (Supported by DDx.)
  - Foodborne toxin-mediated illness — Moderate likelihood: prominent vomiting and possible clustering could reflect a common exposure; less clear history of shared meal. (Supported by DDx.)
- Possible complications / alternative concerns:
  - Dehydration is a concern due to persistent vomiting and inability to retain fluids (DDx notes dehydration as possible complication).
  - Appendicitis considered low likelihood by DDx given diarrheal predominance and household outbreak, but periumbilical tenderness noted — surgical cause unlikely but should be considered if focal worsening or peritoneal signs develop.
- Conflicts/uncertainty: No substantive conflicts between transcript and DDx; objective vitals and examination findings are lacking.

Management Plan
- management_plan_main_or_not_recorded:
  - Urgent in-person clinic appointment recommended to assess hydration and provide same-day stool sample collection for microbiology (arranged via support line per clinician).
  - Continue oral rehydration solution in very small, frequent sips to minimize vomiting.
  - Dietary advice: if eating, stick to very light bland foods (toast, biscuits). Avoid fruit, vegetables, milk while symptomatic as per clinician advice.
  - If symptoms worsen (increasing vomiting, dizziness, reduced urine output, inability to tolerate any fluids), attend A&E urgently for rehydration (IV fluids) and further assessment.
  - If stool testing identifies a bacterial pathogen requiring treatment, targeted medication may be prescribed per clinician guidance.
  - Follow-up arranged via appointment/support line; patient advised to monitor hydration and return if deteriorates.
  - Support staff will book urgent clinic appointment as discussed.
- Consider:
  - Pathology tests as above: Stool microbiology/stool sample for culture/PCR recommended and to be sent from clinic. Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Viral gastroenteritis (e.g., norovirus) — High likelihood.
  - Justification: Acute vomiting and watery diarrhoea for 3 days, subjective fever, household contact and reported school outbreak, no blood in stool; classical presentation.
- Bacterial gastroenteritis (e.g., Salmonella, Campylobacter, pathogenic E. coli) — Moderate likelihood.
  - Justification: Fever and ongoing symptoms not improving with ORS; clinician recommended stool testing to exclude treatable bacterial causes.
- Foodborne toxin (preformed toxins such as Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus cereus) — Moderate likelihood.
  - Justification: Prominent vomiting and possible clustering; less clear history of shared meal and some toxin illnesses have shorter duration.
